UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                        BEFORE THE
                          FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Southern Indiana Gas and Electric                             )
Company                                                       )
                                                              )            Docket No. EL26-38-000
v.                                                            )
                                                              )
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.                )


     MOTION TO INTERVENE AND COMMENTS OF THE OFFICE OF THE ILLINOIS
                          ATTORNEY GENERAL

           Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”), 18 C.F.R. § 385.214(b), the People of the

State of Illinois, by its Attorney General, Kwame Raoul (the "People" or “IL OAG”), request to

intervene in the above-captioned proceeding. Additionally, pursuant to Rule 211 of the

Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, the IL OAG submits these comments in response

to the Complaint filed by Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company d/b/a CenterPoint Energy

Indiana South (“SIGE” or “Company”) against Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.

(“MISO”) on January 5, 2026 (the “Complaint”). The IL OAG requests that the Commission grant

its motion to intervene and accept the comments on the Complaint submitted herein.

I.         MOTION TO INTERVENE

           Illinois law provides that the Illinois Attorney General "shall have the power and duty on

behalf of the people of the State to intervene in, initiate, enforce, and defend all legal proceedings

on matters relating to the provision, marketing, and sale of electric . . . service whenever the

Attorney General determines that such action is necessary to promote or protect the rights and

interests of all Illinois citizens, classes of customers, and users of electric . . . . services.” 1 Illinois


1
    15 ILCS 205/6.5(c).

                                                     1
 law also provides that the “Attorney General shall be a party as a matter of right to all proceedings,

investigations, and related matters involving the provision of electric, natural gas, water, and

telecommunications services before the Illinois Commerce Commission, the courts, and other

public bodies." 2

        The People satisfy the requirements of Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice

and Procedure that an intervenor have or represent “an interest which may be directly affected by

the outcome of the proceeding, including any interest as a . . . consumer.” 3 The People represent

Illinois ratepayers in MISO who may pay the charges associated with Unit 2 of the F.B. Culley

Generating Station spread over the MISO north/central region. Accordingly, the People request

that the Commission grant this Motion to Intervene in this proceeding.

II.     COMMENTS

        In its Complaint, SIGE seeks a mechanism for the Company to obtain rate recovery under

Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) for the costs of operating Unit 2 of the F.B.

Culley Generating Station (“Culley Unit 2”), which was scheduled to cease operations on

December 31, 2025. 4 The unit is remaining open due to the Department of Energy’s Order on

December 23, 2025. 5 SIGE is requesting the same recovery mechanism that was approved by

FERC for Consumers Energy Company for operation of the J.H Campbell Generating Plant

(“Campbell Plant”). 6

                                                      2
         The IL OAG represents the People of the State of Illinois 7 and their interest in receiving

reliable electric services at the least possible cost. 8 Ratepayers in central and southern Illinois may

be subject to the costs of keeping Culley Unit 2 open because they are located in the MISO

north/central region.

        Relying on the Federal Power Act Section 202(c) 9 and Section 301(b) of the Department

of Energy Organization Act 10, the Department of Energy stated that an emergency exists in the

Midwest region of the United States and ordered Culley Unit 2 to remain open. 11 Section 202(c),

however, is subject to certain conditions where “an emergency exists by reason of a sudden

increase in the demand for electric energy, or a shortage of electric energy or of facilities for the

generation or transmission of electric energy or of fuel or water for generating facilities…” 12

Importantly, the DOE Order is subject to rehearing, and its legality will likely be challenged

outside of FERC, which puts this proceeding into question.

        The primary issues in this proceeding are costs and cost allocation. Assuming the DOE has

the legal authority to order Culley Unit 2 to remain open, which the IL OAG does not concede,

FERC should order a MISO stakeholder proceeding to ensure that ratepayers will have a role in

determining cost allocation and to ensure that both costs and rates are just and reasonable.

(“PJM”). Central, and Southern Illinois are encompassed by MISO Local Resource Zone 4 and a small portion of

serving entity for Illinois electricity customers in Northern Illinois, is encompassed by PJM’s ComEd Zone. See PJM
Open Access Transmission Tariff, Attachment J, PJM Transmission Zones, https://agreements.pjm.com/oatt/4443.

         A.       Under the assumption that the DOE Order stands, FERC should order MISO
                 to develop a stakeholder process to ensure that ratepayers subject to the Order
                 have a forum to address cost allocation and to ensure that rates are just and
                 reasonable.

        There are several states in the MISO region, and more specifically in the north/central

region addressed in the Complaint, whose energy resources and prices will be affected by the DOE

Order. This includes Illinois ratepayers who are already facing high capacity charges, transmission

charges, and energy prices. The costs of running Culley Unit 2 allocated throughout MISO

north/central will only add to the burden ratepayers are already facing. The overall costs to operate

Culley Unit 2 are unknown, but are likely significant, given that the unit was slated to retire. This

would likely include maintenance and repair costs. Synapse Energy Economics, Inc. has estimated

the net cost (gross costs net of MISO market energy revenues) of continuing to operate Culley

Unit 2 under economic dispatch is at least $1.9 million, but it could be over $2 million under a

must-run commitment status (meaning it is required to run regardless of whether it would be

economic to do so) over the 90 days covered by the DOE Order. 13 Further costs would continue

to accrue if the order is extended.

        FERC should require a MISO stakeholder process that is fair to consumers. Primarily,

FERC should order the stakeholder process to ensure that the charges associated with Culley Unit

2 and cost allocation are based on the principle of cost causation where the cost causers are the

cost payers. “FERC is not authorized to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of utilities

to pay for facilities from which its members derive no benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation

to the costs sought to be shifted to its members.” 14 FERC must ensure that cost recovery and cost

 allocation are just and reasonable, particularly when there are ratepayers who are not benefitting

from, nor causing, the costs.

        Notably, the DOE Order is only effective for 90 days, although the DOE could seek to

extend the Order beyond the 90 days. For example, the Campbell 202(c) Order has already been

extended by the DOE twice following the initial order. 15 Approving SIGE’s request without regard

to other pending requests for ratemaking for DOE Orders or its long term impact would constitute

a piecemeal approach and deny MISO, stakeholders, and the Commission the opportunity to

address the rate issues associated with the DOE orders comprehensively. The DOE has

demonstrated that it may extend and may institute new 202(c) orders, and the MISO region could

be subject to future orders, including orders affecting plants in Illinois. 16 A stakeholder process at

MISO, to address how plants such as Culley Unit 2 will be compensated, would allow stakeholders

to address 202(c) orders more efficiently than repeated filings and continuous litigation at FERC.

        Under the Company’s proposed approach, costs would be spread across MISO’s

north/central region without determining the reliability benefit for those ratepayers. Unlike in

MISO, when this situation occurred in PJM for the Eddystone Plant, PJM and its members initiated

a Critical Issue Fast Path process, along with PJM states and other stakeholders, to develop a cost

recovery mechanism, as the PJM Tariff did not adequately cover this issue. 17 This allowed for

stakeholder feedback prior to PJM’s cost allocation filing in which it requested approval of its cost

allocation and revisions to its tariff to add a Responsibility to Pay 202(c) Charge. 18 FERC should

 order a similar process for MISO prior to approval of SIGE’s filing. A MISO stakeholder process

will allow for state and ratepayer engagement and transparent analysis of costs and benefits, which

is necessary before costs are imposed on ratepayers in MISO.

III.    CONCLUSION

        WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, the Office of the Illinois Attorney General

respectfully requests that the Commission deny the Complaint and order a stakeholder process at

MISO to address cost allocation for 202(c) orders.
